Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
October 26, 2026
2 min read

Today, we’re launching “Polar Peaks”, our third quest in the AI Quests series, created by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning to teach students how AI works and how to use it responsibly. AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges.

More than 400,000 quests have been completed to date, localized to 10 languages. Alongside the new quest, we’re also releasing training modules for teachers.

Polar Peaks: A journey to map the human brain

In the first two quests, students tackle flood forecasting and eye disease detection, inspired by Google Research’s Flood Forecasting initiative and AI model for diabetic retinopathy screening. Our newest quest, “Polar Peaks,” has students travel to the frontiers of neuroscience and see how AI can speed up scientific research.

With the guidance of in-game mentors, students scan and map the neurons in the brain to better understand the game character’s memory loss. They complete tasks like data cleaning and model testing, learning firsthand that AI requires careful human oversight and critical thinking.

The quest is inspired by over a decade of our research in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete fruit fly brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date.

Training modules: Tools for teaching AI literacy

Teachers play a critical role in bringing the quests to life and fitting them into their existing classroom curriculum. We’re rolling out new dedicated teacher training modules to help educators reinforce key AI literacy concepts and use AI Quests for learning and discussion. These are launching within the Google AI Educator Series. The modules for Quest #1 and #2 are accessible here. The training module for Quest #3 will follow next month.

Earlier this year, AI Quests won a 2026 Webby Award for AI Education, Learning & Training, and Best Global K–12 Learning Solution at the ETIH Innovation Awards. We’ll continue working with educators and partners to bring more quests to more classrooms this school year.

Cypress Blog
How to choose the right Cypress plugins for your project
November 2, 2026
16 min read

You need your tests to do something Cypress doesn’t do on its own, such as waiting for a sign-up email or comparing a screenshot against an approved baseline. A search turns up several plugins that claim to handle it, and integrating the plugin only takes a few minutes. Finding out you integrated the wrong one takes longer, because the problems rarely show up on the day you install it. They show up when a CI job ignores your tag filter and runs the whole suite, or when the plugin blocks your next Cypress upgrade, or when Cypress runs slower until you disable that one plugin.

Integrating a plugin only takes a few minutes. Finding out you integrated the wrong one takes longer.

A Cypress plugin is a package that adds functionality to your Cypress test suite: custom commands, a preprocessor, visual or accessibility checks, a CI integration, or a reporter. Most are npm packages that you install and update separately from Cypress, so each one is a dependency your team maintains. Cypress doesn’t formally review vendor or community plugins, so you decide what goes into your suite.

The Cypress plugin directory helps with that choice. It groups official, vendor, and community plugins by where they fit in your test suite, and each card shows who maintains the plugin, when it last published, and which Cypress versions it declares support for. Those signals, plus a few questions about your own project, tell you whether a plugin belongs in your suite before you install it.

Not every entry in the directory is an npm plugin. Its AI tooling category lists Cypress AI Skills, which help AI coding assistants write, explain, and fix Cypress tests, and the Cloud MCP server, which gives those assistants your Cypress Cloud test data. The directory also lists CI integrations such as the CircleCI orb, the Cypress GitHub Action, Docker images, editor extensions, and Cypress Cloud features. Each of these sets up in its own way, so follow its linked docs. The npm-specific advice in this post, such as peer ranges and setupNodeEvents, applies to the npm packages.

10 min read
Key Takeaways
Generative AI in software testing creates and analyzes test assets. That includes test cases, scripts, test data, and failure summaries.
Faster test generation isn’t stronger verification. Code and tests written from the same prompt can share the same blind spots.
The author can’t be the only verifier. AI-generated code needs independent quality criteria and evidence.
Use generative AI as a challenger, not the final judge. It works best for adversarial test ideas, change mapping, and failure triage.
Agentic testing connects the full lifecycle. It links authoring, execution, failure analysis, and recovery. People still own release decisions.

Generative AI in software testing uses AI to create and analyze test assets. These outputs can include test cases, automation scripts, test data, assertions, documentation, and failure summaries.

Used well, generative AI can help teams expand coverage and respond faster to software changes.

Faster test generation does not automatically produce stronger verification.

As AI coding agents increase the volume of code entering development pipelines, engineering teams need an independent way to determine whether those changes meet their quality standards.

If the same assumptions shape both the code and its tests, teams risk releasing defects with a misleading sense of confidence.

Generative AI can support authoring, failure analysis, and maintenance. Agentic systems can connect those capabilities to execution and recovery, while teams retain control over quality, intent and release decisions.

What Is Generative AI in Software Testing?

Generative AI refers to models that produce new content based on prompts, source material, and other context. In software testing, that content might include:

Test scenarios derived from requirements
Automated test scripts
Assertions for expected application behavior
Test data and edge-case ideas
Explanations of test failures
Suggested updates for broken tests
Summaries of release risk and coverage

A practical generative AI in software testing framework connects these outputs to quality goals. A team might ask AI to convert a user story into scenarios, explain a regression, or identify workflows affected by a change.

This differs from testing applications that contain generative AI features, which requires evaluating nondeterministic outputs, model behavior, safety, and reliability. Teams testing AI features can use model calls within their tests.

Tip: Our guide to integrating generative AI into end-to-end testing includes examples of generated inputs and AI-assisted evaluation of outputs.

Why AI-Generated Code Can Create a Verification Problem

AI coding agents can help developers produce features, refactor code, and resolve issues faster. The resulting increase in delivery throughput also raises the amount of code that needs to be verified.

The central concern is independence. If an AI system writes code and then generates tests from the same instructions, both outputs may inherit the same misunderstanding. A requirement omitted from the prompt may be absent from the implementation and its test. The generated test may also mirror the code's structure rather than validate the intended user outcome.

prompt: What is red-teaming in AI safety?
response: AI Red Teaming is a systematic security testing discipline that forces a deployed Large Language Model (LLM) or integrated AI system to bypass its safety controls, leak confidential data, or execute unauthorized actions.Unlike traditional network penetration testing, which targets firewalls or SQL injection, AI red teaming targets the natural-language parsing layer and semantic guardrails. The core goal is to identify vulnerabilities where the AI fails to adhere to its intended safety policies.Key Characteristics  Target: It tests the integrated system (Model + Guardrails + Tools + RAG), not just the bare model.  Input Treatment: Every natural-language input is treated as a potential injection vector, similar to how QA engineers treat API inputs for standard security testing.  Methodology: It involves using adversarial datasets and automated scripts to simulate attacks that a malicious user might perform.Common Attack VectorsAccording to the provided knowledge base, red teaming focuses on several primary vectors: Direct Prompt Injection: User text overrides the system prompt, leading to system prompt leakage. Indirect Prompt Injection: Malicious payloads hidden in external content (PDFs, web pages, emails) that trigger unauthorized tool calls or data leakage. Jailbreaks: Bypassing content/safety policies via persona attacks or roleplay to generate unsafe outputs. Data Leakage/Extraction: Using reverse psychology or roleplay to reveal training data, PII, or secret keys. Safety-Framing Bypass: Multi-turn reframing of a harmful request as a "protective" or educational query (e.g., "List what NOT to do") to trick the model into enumerating harmful information (e.g., CBRN recipes) despite refusing a direct ask. Tool Abuse/Excessive Agency: Tricking agentic systems into calling unauthorized tools or executing actions beyond their intended scope.Operational Principles  Continuous Automation: Manual red teaming finds novel exploits but does not scale. Red teaming must be automated and run continuously in CI/CD and production to catch regressions.  Versioned Adversarial Datasets: Teams maintain a growing library of attack patterns that are versioned and re-tested with every new model update or prompt change.  Separation from Edge Cases: Red-team examples are distinct from "edge cases" (real users doing weird things). Red-team suites are typically gated at zero failures because any successful bypass is considered a critical security vulnerability, whereas edge cases may be acceptable trade-offs depending on product requirements.In summary, AI red teaming is the proactive, adversarial testing process required to ensure that LLM-based applications remain secure against exploitation of their natural language interfaces and integrated tooling.Supervisor→RAG AgentSourcesAI Red Teaming.md 0.61Advanced LLM Red Teaming and Adversarial Testing Strategies for QA Engineers.docx 0.60End-to-End First Eval Strategy.md 0.54OWASP LLM Top 10.md 0.54Combinatorial AI Testing.md 0.52
